aboutAuthor: John Brooks (1920–1993) was a New Yorker business writer whose long-form narratives defined financial journalism. Bill Gates calls Business Adventures his favorite business book; Warren Buffett borrowed it from Gates and never gave it back.

points.heading: The Ford Edsel: marketing can't save the wrong product
points.body: Ford spent $350 million and years of consumer research building the 'perfect' car — and America laughed at it. The Edsel failed because committees designed it by consensus and hype raised expectations to impossible heights. Research tells you what people want only if you build what they actually asked for.

points.heading: The Flash Crash of 1962
points.body: In May 1962, the Dow fell 6% in three days with no news at all. Brooks shows markets are made of people whose fear feeds on itself — a lesson repeated verbatim in every flash crash since. When everyone sells because everyone else is selling, price reveals panic, not value.

points.heading: Xerox Xerox: success breeds complacency
points.body: Xerox's copying monopoly generated so much cash that its famous Palo Alto research lab's inventions were ignored — including the graphical interface later stolen by Apple. Companies that stop fearing their future stop inventing it.

points.heading: The Texas Gulf Sulphur insider scandal
points.body: Executives quietly bought stock after striking rich ore but before announcing the find. The SEC case that followed created modern rules on insider trading. Markets run on trust; when insiders exploit private information, everyone else is just donating.

points.heading: Piggly Wiggly: one man versus the Street
points.body: Grocery founder Clarence Saunders tried to corner his own company's stock to punish Wall Street short sellers — and lost everything. The episode shows how leverage turns conviction into catastrophe regardless of who is right.

points.heading: Goodwill is a real balance-sheet item
points.body: Brooks's account of General Electric's price-fixing scandal shows how 'everyone does it' reasoning spreads through an organization. Culture is what happens when no policy is watching; scandals are culture made visible.

insights: The book collects twelve New Yorker essays published between 1959 and 1969.
Gates says almost nothing in the book feels dated despite being written decades ago.
'The Impacted Philosophers' — Brooks on oil-industry communication failures — remains a cult favorite.
conclusion: Business Adventures proves that markets never change, only their costumes. Human greed, herd behavior, and hubris produced every disaster Brooks chronicled — and reading them is the cheapest insurance an investor or executive will ever buy.
